facts.statement: The study compared 51 people with obsessive-compulsive disorder (39 men) to 59 healthy controls (37 men) to look at how the cerebellum connects with the rest of the brain.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: Researchers used computer simulations of brain damage and network grouping techniques to see which parts of the cerebellum support goal-directed versus habitual behavior.
facts.subject: computational

facts.statement: In both the patient and control groups, removing the Crus I/II area of the cerebellum disrupted how the brain networks work together, but removing lobules V/VI only had this effect in the healthy controls.
facts.subject: computational

facts.statement: The analysis showed that the Crus I/II region groups with networks for goal-directed actions, while lobules V/VI group with networks for habitual actions.
facts.subject: computational

facts.statement: People with OCD showed stronger connections within the brain's habitual action network, and this strength was linked to how severe their compulsive symptoms were.
facts.subject: humans
